Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act;

Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Childrenâ€™s Health

Dear Dr. Oz: 
 
On behalf of the American Society of Pediatric Nephrology (ASPN), thank you for the 
opportunity to submit comments on the Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for 
Drugs proposed rule. ASPN strongly supports the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Servicesâ€™ 
(CMS) and the Ofï¬ce of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technologyâ€™s efforts to 
modernize and streamline prior authorization processes, reduce administrative burden on 
providers and families, and improve timely access to medically necessary prescription drugs.  
Founded in 1969, ASPN is a professional society composed of pediatric nephrologists whose 
goal is to promote optimal care for children with kidney disease and to disseminate advances in 
the clinical practice and basic science of pediatric nephrology. ASPN currently has over 700 
members, making it the primary representative of the Pediatric Nephrology community in North 
America. 
An estimated 150,000 children and adolescents currently suffer from kidney disease; about 
10,000 of them suffer from chronic kidney failure, receive chronic dialysis, or have a kidney 
transplant. Children with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) are the only children automatically 
eligible for Medicare, and approximately one-third are covered by the program with another third 
covered by Medicaid and the remaining third covered by private insurance. Children and 
adolescents undergoing dialysis or transplants are unique, and very different from adults. The 
causes for ESKD in children predominantly include congenital abnormalities, glomerular 
diseases and rare genetic disorders, not hypertension and diabetes as seen in adults 
undergoing the same treatment. Children with ESKD also suffer from impaired growth and 
development, including impaired neurocognitive development. They also have different drug 
metabolism, which changes over time as they grow to be adults. In addition, many children with 
chronic kidney disease experience feeding and swallowing disorders which necessitate liquid 
formulations of medications, often administered via nasogastric tubes or gastric tubes. 
 
These differences between children and adults with kidney disease, and speciï¬cally ESKD, are 
particularly important when considering prior authorization policies, which may delay access to 
medically appropriate care and therapies for pediatric patients. These children regularly require 
pediatric-speciï¬c medications and formulations to manage their complex condition or maintain 
their transplanted kidneys. Delays caused by inefï¬cient or duplicative prior authorization 
requirements can have profound clinical consequences for children.  
 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs  
After addressing prior authorization for services in 2024, CMS proposes to include drugs in prior 
authorization interoperability requirements and processes in this proposal. ASPN recommends 
that CMS adopt the proposal to adopt electronic prior authorization for drugs as this will reduce 
the administrative burden associated with current manual workï¬‚ows. Adopting standardized 
electronic prior authorization processes and improving interoperability has the potential to make 
the system more efï¬cient for patients and providers, which will ultimately improve access to 
clinically appropriate therapies. 
As previously stated, pediatric nephrologists treat children on Medicare, Medicaid, and private 
plans, all with differing prior authorization process. Children with kidney disease often rely on 
therapies used to treat rare disorders for which treatment interruptions can have serious long-
term consequences. Prior authorization variability across states and plans creates signiï¬cant 
inequities in access to care. ASPN encourages CMS to work collaboratively with pediatric 
specialists, rare disease organizations, and patient advocates to identify opportunities for 
standardization and exemptions for clinically essential therapies with limited or no therapeutic 
alternatives.  Unfortunately, in clinical practice, due to the nature of rare conditions and small 
populations, many treatments used for children with chronic kidney disease are used off-label 
without speciï¬c FDA approved indications. Lacking the level of evidence often found in adult 
studies, payers often automatically deny potential lifesaving medications in children, leading to 
long appeals processes and delays in optimal care â€“ even when there are no treatments FDA-
approved for a speciï¬c diagnosis. ASPN encourages CMS to work with our community partners 
to create innovative pathways to expedite these types of approvals. 
ASPN also strongly recommends that CMS support standardization of electronic prior 
authorization processes across the programs within its jurisdiction. Our members routinely 
navigate payer and plan speciï¬c forms, submission requirements, and documentation 
standards. The lack of standardization delays care unnecessarily and takes valuable time away 
from patient care. CMS should promote alignment around core clinical data elements, which are 
essential to efï¬cient workï¬‚ows, and to allow for prompt decisions on prior authorization 
requests. Core clinical data elements for drug prior authorization requests include items like 
diagnoses, biomarker and laboratory test results, prior treatment history and therapy failures, 
contraindications, and adverse reactions.  
Reporting Metrics and Decision Timeframes 
We recommend that CMS ï¬nalize the proposed timelines for prior authorization decisions: 
standard requests to be turned around in 72 hours and expedited requests in 24 hours. 
However, we do request clariï¬cation that this policy applies 24 hours a day, seven days a week. 
The implementation of this policy would represent a meaningful improvement over existing 
processes and could help reduce treatment delays that frequently disrupt care. While these 
proposed timelines are an important step forward, ASPN encourages CMS to continue 
evaluating opportunities to further streamline approvals that are clinically routine, long-
established, or necessary for chronic disease management in the pediatric and adult 
populations. For example, we urge CMS to move towards real-time approval or denials. Real-
time decisions, while a child and their caregiver and provider are in the same room, will increase 
shared decision-making, improve patient care, and improve timely access to needed therapies 
and drugs.  
Furthermore, ASPN urges CMS to address the requirements for repeated reauthorizations 
across the programs in its jurisdiction. Children with chronic kidney disease often remain on the 
same therapies for years but the appropriate dosing may change, yet providers and families 
must repeatedly navigate unnecessary prior authorizations that interrupt continuity of care and 
divert clinician time away from patient care.   
Our members report that the appeals process is one of the most burdensome and time-
consuming parts of the prior authorization process. Speciï¬cally, ASPN members have voiced 
challenges with the peer-to-peer appeal requests as they are more time consuming, especially if 
providers miss the initial 24-hour window post denial to submit this request. ASPN recommends 
that CMS revisit the appeals process. Our members note that some of the longest care delays 
are created when they appeal a prior authorization decision, with plans asking for additional 
documentation, chart notes, or other types of information to decide. We recommend that CMS 
strengthen requirements for appeal timeliness, require timely escalation to qualiï¬ed clinical 
reviewers, and provide transparency regarding appeal outcomes as well as ensuring that a 
pediatrician participate in the review of appeals submitted for medications and formulas required 
to treat children.  
Finally, we support CMSâ€™s efforts to improve transparency through public reporting of prior 
authorization metrics.  To be meaningful in the pediatric population, we recommend that this be 
provided at the drug level and include information on approval rates, denial rates, appeal 
outcomes, and turnaround times. We recommend that these metrics be reported for the 
following drugs, some of the most prescribed to children with kidney disease:

Many of these agents are older, inexpensive drugs. Repeated prior authorizations for these 
agents in the pediatric population â€“ particularly for minor dose changes in response to growth or 
lab results - are particularly burdensome and delay care for these vulnerable children. 
CMS should also establish robust enforcement mechanisms to ensure compliance with 
turnaround time requirements and denial transparency standards. Without meaningful oversight 
and accountability, shorter timelines alone may not translate into improved patient access. 
Should you require additional information or have any questions, please contact Erika Miller,

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Society of Pediatric Nephrology (ASPN); signed by Sandra Amaral, MD, MHS, President.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Healthcare Provider specialty society.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** ASPN represents more than 700 pediatric nephrologists and describes expertise caring for children with kidney disease, chronic kidney failure, dialysis, and kidney transplantation.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ASPN strongly supports CMS efforts to modernize drug prior authorization through standardized electronic processes because pediatric nephrology patients face serious clinical consequences from delayed medications and formulations. The commenter recommends finalizing drug electronic prior authorization and decision timelines, while adding pediatric-focused standardization, exemptions or expedited pathways for clinically essential and off-label rare-disease therapies, stronger appeals standards, drug-level reporting, and enforcement.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY/GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No specific CFR citations are cited. The commenter references the proposed rule CMS-0062-P and proposed 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited prior authorization timeframes.
- **Standards referenced:** Standardized electronic prior authorization, interoperability, payer-plan clinical data elements. The comment does not name specific FHIR IGs, NCPDP standards, HL7 standards, or HIPAA transaction standards.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Adopt electronic prior authorization for drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** ASPN states that current manual workflows impose administrative burden and delay access to clinically appropriate pediatric kidney disease therapies.
- **Specific request:** CMS should adopt the proposal to include drugs in electronic prior authorization requirements and promote standardized processes across programs under CMS jurisdiction.

**Topic 2: Pediatric rare disease and off-label therapy pathways**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PATIENT-ACCESS/GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Children with kidney disease often need pediatric-specific formulations, rare-disease therapies, and off-label uses where FDA-approved alternatives do not exist; automatic denials can trigger long appeals and clinically harmful delays.
- **Specific request:** CMS should collaborate with pediatric specialists, rare disease organizations, and patient advocates to create standardization, exemptions, and innovative expedited approval pathways for clinically essential therapies with limited or no alternatives.

**Topic 3: Standard clinical data elements**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Variation in plan-specific forms, submission requirements, and documentation standards delays care and diverts clinician time.
- **Specific request:** CMS should align payer requirements around core clinical data elements, including diagnoses, biomarkers, laboratory results, prior treatment history, therapy failures, contraindications, and adverse reactions.

**Topic 4: Decision timeframes and real-time decisions**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with clarification
- **Rationale:** The proposed 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited timelines would reduce treatment delays, but pediatric care can require decisions while provider, caregiver, and child are together.
- **Specific request:** CMS should finalize the timeframes, clarify that they operate 24 hours a day and seven days a week, and continue moving toward real-time approvals or denials for routine or chronic disease therapies.

**Topic 5: Reauthorizations and appeals**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Repeated prior authorizations for long-term therapies and minor pediatric dose changes disrupt continuity of care; appeals and peer-to-peer requests create some of the longest care delays.
- **Specific request:** CMS should address repeated reauthorization requirements, strengthen appeal timeliness, require escalation to qualified clinical reviewers, ensure pediatrician participation in pediatric medication/formula appeals, and improve appeal outcome transparency.

**Topic 6: Public reporting and enforcement**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Reporting must be granular enough to show pediatric access problems, especially for older and inexpensive drugs that still face burdensome repeated authorization.
- **Specific request:** CMS should require drug-level metrics including approval rates, denial rates, appeal outcomes, and turnaround times for pediatric kidney disease medications, and establish enforcement mechanisms for turnaround-time and denial-transparency compliance.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16:** ASPN responds indirectly by requesting stronger denial and appeal transparency, including reporting appeal outcomes and ensuring pediatric expertise in appeals for children.
- **S17:** The commenter does not discuss structured denial codes directly, but supports standardized clinical data elements and transparency that could support structured denial and appeal reporting.
- **S20:** ASPN supports finalizing 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited prior authorization timelines and asks CMS to clarify that the policy applies 24/7.
- **S21:** ASPN supports electronic prior authorization for drugs and views the proposed timelines as meaningful improvements, while recommending continued movement toward real-time decisions.
- **S29:** ASPN recommends drug-level reporting metrics, specifically approval rates, denial rates, appeal outcomes, and turnaround times for medications frequently prescribed to children with kidney disease.
- **S34/S35:** ASPN supports public reporting of prior authorization metrics and asks that reporting be meaningful for pediatric populations, but does not specify frequency or aggregation methodology.
- **S66-S82:** The comment raises general prior authorization concerns for chronic pediatric kidney disease, rare disease therapies, reauthorizations, appeals, and access to medically necessary drugs.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic prior authorization for drugs to reduce manual workflows and administrative burden.
2. Standardize prior authorization requirements across CMS-regulated programs and payers.
3. Create pediatric and rare-disease pathways, including exemptions or expedited approval for essential therapies with limited alternatives.
4. Align payer requirements around core clinical data elements needed for drug prior authorization.
5. Finalize 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited decision timeframes and clarify they apply 24/7.
6. Move toward real-time approvals or denials for routine, established, or chronic disease therapies.
7. Reduce unnecessary repeated reauthorizations for long-term pediatric therapies and dose changes.
8. Strengthen appeal timeliness, escalation to qualified reviewers, pediatrician involvement, and appeal outcome transparency.
9. Require drug-level public reporting of approval rates, denial rates, appeal outcomes, and turnaround times for pediatric kidney disease medications.
10. Establish meaningful enforcement mechanisms for turnaround-time and denial-transparency standards.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Pediatric kidney disease patients face delayed access to medically necessary drugs, rare-disease therapies, off-label pediatric uses, liquid formulations, and chronic maintenance medications.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment interruptions, long-term clinical consequences, disrupted transplant or dialysis care, inequitable access across states and plans, and reduced clinician time for patient care.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payer-specific forms, differing submission requirements, inconsistent documentation standards, repeated reauthorizations, burdensome peer-to-peer appeals, and lack of pediatric expertise in review.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** ASPN states that about 150,000 children and adolescents have kidney disease; about 10,000 have chronic kidney failure, dialysis, or kidney transplantation; coverage is roughly split among Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No formal studies are cited.
- **Examples provided:** The commenter lists pediatric kidney disease medications and formulations, including amlodipine suspension, calcitriol, cysteamine, enalapril suspension, Epogen/Darbepoetin, growth hormone, IVIG, rituximab/obinutuzumab, sevelamer/Renvela, sparsentan, spironolactone oral suspension, and Valcyte.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Pediatric patients with kidney disease and ESKD, families/caregivers, pediatric nephrologists, pediatric specialists, rare disease organizations, payers, Medicaid/Medicare programs, and private plans.
- **Economic implications:** The comment emphasizes administrative cost and clinician time burden rather than quantified dollar impacts; it notes that many affected drugs are older and inexpensive despite repeated authorization burden.
- **Technical feasibility:** ASPN views standardized electronic prior authorization as feasible and beneficial, but stresses the need for aligned data elements and consistent requirements.
- **Patient care impact:** Faster and more standardized prior authorization could reduce treatment delays, improve continuity of care, support shared decision-making, and improve access to clinically necessary pediatric therapies.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, clinical, collaborative, and patient-access focused.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "ASPN strongly supports" CMS and ONC efforts to modernize prior authorization. - Context: Opening statement of overall support.
2. "Delays caused by inefficient or duplicative prior authorization requirements can have profound clinical consequences for children." - Context: Pediatric kidney disease access risk.
3. "ASPN recommends that CMS adopt the proposal to adopt electronic prior authorization for drugs." - Context: Direct support for drug ePA.
4. "We urge CMS to move towards real-time approval or denials." - Context: Recommendation to go beyond proposed timelines.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - ASPN supports 72-hour and 24-hour timelines, seeks 24/7 clarification, and urges real-time decisions.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment highlights administrative burden and clinician time costs, especially for reauthorizations and appeals.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Pediatric nephrologists face payer-specific forms, peer-to-peer appeals, documentation demands, and repeated reauthorization work.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - ASPN states that variability across states and plans creates inequities in access for children with kidney disease.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The commenter supports standardization around core clinical data elements to make electronic workflows efficient.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The central concern is delayed access to medically necessary pediatric kidney disease therapies.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - ASPN asks CMS to work with pediatric specialists, rare disease organizations, and patient advocates.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - ASPN recommends drug-level reporting of approvals, denials, appeals, and turnaround times.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment describes current manual workflows, payer-specific forms, and peer-to-peer appeal processes as problematic.
